Discussion of Results Samples from the Early Trisasic, Permian, and Middle Carboniferous formations were serverely overprinted by BNF. As many as 65% of paleomagnetic data showed only one component directions of BNF as well as random or unstable magnetizations. The maxium unblocking temperature for the BNF component in the hematite-bearing beds studied by us is in the range 600Ž to 650Ž. According to the relaxation time-blocking temperature (t-T) relations of PULLAIAH et al. (1975), this would indicate that the beds acquired a thermoviscous remanence near Curie temperature in the Brunhes. The lack of any evidence of high temperature regional or contact metamorphism of the formations, however, indicates that the remagnetization process of hematite-bearing beds most likely involved the chemical precipitation or alteration of hematite, following the results of KENT and MILLER (1987) and WITTE and KENT (1991), rather than a thermoviscous resetting of existing hematite. EINLEITUNG Die paläomagnetische Untersuchung permischer Rotsedimente der Gurk- taler Decke erfolgte in den Vorkommen des Krappfeldes und der St. Pauler Berge (Abb. 1 und 2). In beiden Gebieten lieferten Silt- und Sandsteine des Unterrotliegenden brauchbare Ergebnisse, während im Permoskyth- sandstein keine einheitliche fossile Remanenzrichtung festgestellt werden konnte. Hier verhinderten bei der Sedimentation zu grobe Korngrößen eine Einregelung der ferromagnetischen Partikel parallel zum Erdfeld. SYMONS Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada N9B 3P4 AND D. F. SANGSTER Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada KIA OE8 Abstract In the Central Missouri barite district, barite samples were taken from four barite deposits and carbonate samples from the Lower Ordovician Jefferson City and Gasconade Dolomites in two road cuts and from the Mississippian Burlington Limestone in a quarry. INTRODUCTION The study area is located in the NW part of the Himalayan range in Hazara (Pakistan) and Azad Kashmir. The large-scale tectonic structure of the region is characterized by a structural reentrant or syntaxial bend, the Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis (HKS). Because of its complex composition and key position for the geology of the northwestern Himalayas, several very detailed stratigraphic, structural, and petrographical investigations have been undertaken on the HKS [Wadia, 1931; Calkins et al., 1975; Bossart et al., 1988; Bossart and Ottiger, 1989]. This paper presents new paleomagnetic results from three sections (Jhelum, Neelum, and Kaghan valley) across the core of the HKS. One result of previous structural investigations [Bossart et al., 1988] was the observation of increas- ing finite-strain state from south to north in the core of the syntaxis. This result was taken into consider- ation when we prepared the present study. Primary paleomagnetic directions are more likely to be found 104 Bossart et al.: Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis, Rock Magnetic Properties, Pakistan in the southern sections than in the northern ones, where primary directions are obliterated by tectonic strain. Our paleomagnetic approach is therefore twofold. On one hand, the weakly defor

roach is therefore twofold. On one hand, the weakly deformed south- ernmost section in the Jhelum valley is useful for a regional paleogeographic and tectonic interpretation, using the primary paleomagnetic directions for determination of the paleolatitude and relative rota- tions of the Murree formation. This paleomagnetic information leads to a modification of our previous kinematic model for the formation of the syntaxis [Bossart et al., 1988], resulting in a more unique solution. On the other hand, the broad spectrum of natural strains preserved in the rocks gives informa- tion about progressive deformation. By measuring the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS), a quali- tative agreement of the strains observed in the field and those derived from magnetic fabrics was ob- tained. Finally, a deformation path from south to north is suggested, which refers to the more local deformational aspect of the syntaxis. 2. GEOLOGICAL REVIEW 2.1. The Tectonic Structure of the Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis The Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis consists of a series of overlapping thrust sheets. They are made up of various Precambrian, Paleozoic, and Mesozoic formations which have been overthrust on Tertiary molasse deposits, known as the Murree formation. Two major thrusts can be distinguished: a higher Panja

tern part of the syntaxis has been displaced toward the south some tens of kilometers relative to the eastem part. Greco et al. [1989] have shown that this mylonite shear zone separates the tectonic units of the Lesser and Higher Himalaya and is therefore related to the Main Central Thrust (MCT). The core of the syntaxis (Figure 1) is best inter- preted with a dome model [Bossart et al., 1988]. The two limbs of the domal fold are characterized by a change in the bedding-cleavage relationship: in the Kaghan section, the bedding-cleavage intersection lineations (equals fold axes) dip steeply to the NE, North, and NW, whereas in the Neelum section they dip with intermediate angles to the SE (see stereo- grams of Figure 1). This domal fold in the Murree formation developed by layer compression subper- pendicular to a southwestward overthrust direction. This direction was derived by finite cleavage and stretching lineations in the Murree formation (mineral reorientation parallel to the longest axis of deformed reduction spots). The Murree thrust cuts down the Murree strata from NE to SW. The palaeomagnetic south pole for one remanence was estimated as 165.1°E, 65.7°S (A95 = 11.5°). The direction for the other remanence was not well defined; however samples collected from diamictite bodies within the breccia gave 133.9°E, 33.1°S (A95 = 6.9°) as the probable pole for the overprint. The latter is similar to overprint poles published from central Australia, which are generally attributed to the Alice Springs Orogeny. Magnetization directions interpreted as Permo-Carboniferous were obtained also from the Mt Gee Sinter (a quartz-hematite-rich chemical sedimentary rock which overlies the Radium Ridge Breccias) and from U- mineralized hematitic ironstone bodies within the breccia. The magnetizations of both units were probably coeval with the younger magnetization of the Radium Ridge Breccias. A positive fold test demonstrates that the remanence of the sinter is primary, indicating a major hydrothermal event in the Permo-Carboniferous. It is not clear by how much this event post-dates the deposition of the underlying Radium Ridge Breccias and hematitic ironstone. The latter may be Ordovician or older if earlier monazite U-Pb data are correct, and may have been formed by granit

the Permo-Carboniferous. It is not clear by how much this event post-dates the deposition of the underlying Radium Ridge Breccias and hematitic ironstone. The latter may be Ordovician or older if earlier monazite U-Pb data are correct, and may have been formed by granite-related hydrothermal fluids. In that case, the older remanence in the breccia is also an overprint. Epithermal sinter formation and chemical (rather than purely thermal) resetting of the remanence in the underlying breccia were probably due to deep circulation of oxidized fluids during Permo-Carboniferous tectonic activity. Chemical reaction of these fluids with pre-existing magnetite-bearing ironstone may have been responsible for uranium mineralization during the Permo-Carboniferous. This interpretation is consistent with published textural, isotopic and fluid inclusion data, but an older age for the uranium concentration, as a primary part of the ironstone formation, cannot be excluded. Alternatively, if the monazite data are discarded, the entire hydrothermal process including iron, uranium and silica deposition could have occurred in the Permo-Carboniferous. Key words: hydrothermal, palaeomagnetism, sinter, uranium ore. INTRODUCTION The Mt Painter area, 550 km north of Adelaide in the northern Flinders Ranges of Sout

. The Mt Painter Inlier exposes Middle Proterozoic crystalline basement and is surrounded by Adelaidean (Late Proterozoic) sedimentary sequences. The region has experienced a complex thermal history extending through to present-day hot spring activity. The Phanerozoic thermal history of the inlier was probably influenced by the abundance of unusually uranium-rich highly fractionated alkali-feldspar granite, regarded as Palaeozoic in age (Teale 1979; Teale & Lottermoser 1987; Drexel & Major 1990). The breccia is composed dom- inantly of locally derived basement clasts which are altered and cemented to varying degrees by K-feldspar, quartz and hematite. Breccia is distributed over an area of at least 8 x 10km near the centre of the inlier (Fig. 1), and comprises forms varying from massive breccia piles to funnel-shaped bodies, with water-laid and subaerial chem- ical and mechanical sedimentary strata which are still in a near-horizontal bedding position (Youles 1975; Major 1976; Drexel & Major 1987, 1990; Higgins et al. 1988). The origin of the breccia and contained ores is debated; interpretations ranging from magmatic-hydrothermal activity associated with Ordovician (or younger) granitoid intrusion (Drexel 1980; Lambert et al. 1982), through deep hydrothermal fluid convection driven by t

-temperature supergene processes associated with deep weathering in the Tertiary (Blissett in Coats & Blissett 1971). Any information on the absolute timing of breccia formation and mineralization impacts directly on these widely disparate genetic interpretations. The typically 88 M. IDNURM AND C. A. Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. . The Mt Painter Inlier exposes Middle Proterozoic crystalline basement and is surrounded by Adelaidean (Late Proterozoic) sedimentary sequences. The region has experienced a complex thermal history extending through to present-day hot spring activity. The Phanerozoic thermal history of the inlier was probably influenced by the abundance of unusually uranium-rich highly fractionated alkali-feldspar granite, regarded as Palaeozoic in age (Teale 1979; Teale & Lottermoser 1987; Drexel & Major 1990). (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. the Permo-Carboniferous. It is not clear by how much this event post-dates the deposition of the underlying Radium Ridge Breccias and hematitic ironstone. The latter may be Ordovician or older if earlier monazite U-Pb data are correct, and may have been formed by granite-related hydrothermal fluids. In that case, the older remanence in the breccia is also an overprint. Epithermal sinter formation and chemical (rather than purely thermal) resetting of the remanence in the underlying breccia were probably due to deep circulation of oxidized fluids during Permo-Carboniferous tectonic activity. Chemical reaction of these fluids with pre-existing magnetite-bearing ironstone may have been responsible for uranium mineralization during the Permo-Carboniferous. This interpretation is consistent with published textural, isotopic and fluid inclusion data, but an older age for the uranium concentration, as a primary part of the ironstone formation, cannot be excluded. Alternatively, if the monazite data are discarded, the entire hydrothermal process including iron, uranium and silica deposition could have occurred in the Permo-Carboniferous. Key words: hydrothermal, palaeomagnetism, sinter, uranium ore. INTRODUCTION The Mt Painter area, 550 km north of Adelaide in the northern Flinders Ranges of Sout

. The Mt Painter Inlier exposes Middle Proterozoic crystalline basement and is surrounded by Adelaidean (Late Proterozoic) sedimentary sequences. The region has experienced a complex thermal history extending through to present-day hot spring activity. The Phanerozoic thermal history of the inlier was probably influenced by the abundance of unusually uranium-rich highly fractionated alkali-feldspar granite, regarded as Palaeozoic in age (Teale 1979; Teale & Lottermoser 1987; Drexel & Major 1990). The breccia is composed dom- inantly of locally derived basement clasts which are altered and cemented to varying degrees by K-feldspar, quartz and hematite. Breccia is distributed over an area of at least 8 x 10km near the centre of the inlier (Fig. 1), and comprises forms varying from massive breccia piles to funnel-shaped bodies, with water-laid and subaerial chem- ical and mechanical sedimentary strata which are still in a near-horizontal bedding position (Youles 1975; Major 1976; Drexel & Major 1987, 1990; Higgins et al. 1988). The origin of the breccia and contained ores is debated; interpretations ranging from magmatic-hydrothermal activity associated with Ordovician (or younger) granitoid intrusion (Drexel 1980; Lambert et al. 1982), through deep hydrothermal fluid convection driven by t

-temperature supergene processes associated with deep weathering in the Tertiary (Blissett in Coats & Blissett 1971). Any information on the absolute timing of breccia formation and mineralization impacts directly on these widely disparate genetic interpretations. The typically 88 M. IDNURM AND C. A. Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). GRANITIC BRECCIA Granitic breccia, the dominant breccia type, comprises mainly clasts of local basement granite, gneiss and schist, ranging from house-sized blocks to silt-sized fragments. Sorting

ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). These include, in order of paragenetic sequence: monazite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, magnetite, specular hematite, clear quartz, uraninite, later Cu-Fe-Pb-Zn-sulphide minerals including chalcocite and bornite, followed by carbonate, chlorite, fluorite and later cloudy quartz. Some of the hematite pseudomorphs earlier magnetite (Stillwell & Edwards 1954; Drexel & Major 1990). DIAMICTITE Diamictite occurs in small outcrops and drillhole intersections along a distinct east-west trend (Fig. 1). In sharp contrast to the enclosing granitic breccia, the diamictite contains a variety of well-rounded clasts, including porphyritic volcanic and other rocks that do not occur in the local basement (Fig. 2c). The cobbles are supported by a silty to sandy matrix which is undeformed and unrecrystallized. The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Where exposed in three dimensions, the diamictite bodies show sharp and steep contacts with the granitic breccia, but no contact relations to hematitic breccia or quartz-hematite sinter were observed. The diamictite has been interpreted variably as stratigraphic intercalations of Adelaidean glaciomarine strata (on the basis of their striking lithological similarity with massive Sturtian tillite adjacent to the inlier; Youles 1975,1986); as solid rafts that were introduced tectonically (Drexel & Major 1987, 1990); as pebble-breccia dykes (Drexel & Major 1987); and as soft-sediment intrusive 'dykes'(Sprigg 1989). 90 M. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). GRANITIC BRECCIA Granitic breccia, the dominant breccia type, comprises mainly clasts of local basement granite, gneiss and schist, ranging from house-sized blocks to silt-sized fragments. Sorting

ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). These include, in order of paragenetic sequence: monazite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, magnetite, specular hematite, clear quartz, uraninite, later Cu-Fe-Pb-Zn-sulphide minerals including chalcocite and bornite, followed by carbonate, chlorite, fluorite and later cloudy quartz. The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). GRANITIC BRECCIA Granitic breccia, the dominant breccia type, comprises mainly clasts of local basement granite, gneiss and schist, ranging from house-sized blocks to silt-sized fragments. Sorting

ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). These include, in order of paragenetic sequence: monazite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, magnetite, specular hematite, clear quartz, uraninite, later Cu-Fe-Pb-Zn-sulphide minerals including chalcocite and bornite, followed by carbonate, chlorite, fluorite and later cloudy quartz. Some of the hematite pseudomorphs earlier magnetite (Stillwell & Edwards 1954; Drexel & Major 1990). DIAMICTITE Diamictite occurs in small outcrops and drillhole intersections along a distinct east-west trend (Fig. 1). In sharp contrast to the enclosing granitic breccia, the diamictite contains a variety of well-rounded clasts, including porphyritic volcanic and other rocks that do not occur in the local basement (Fig. 2c). The cobbles are supported by a silty to sandy matrix which is undeformed and unrecrystallized. The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Where exposed in three dimensions, the diamictite bodies show sharp and steep contacts with the granitic breccia, but no contact relations to hematitic breccia or quartz-hematite sinter were observed. The diamictite has been interpreted variably as stratigraphic intercalations of Adelaidean glaciomarine strata (on the basis of their striking lithological similarity with massive Sturtian tillite adjacent to the inlier; Youles 1975,1986); as solid rafts that were introduced tectonically (Drexel & Major 1987, 1990); as pebble-breccia dykes (Drexel & Major 1987); and as soft-sediment intrusive 'dykes'(Sprigg 1989). 90 M. Silurian andesites and tuffs The magnetization structure of the Silurian volcanics can be divided into two categories, termed Type 1 (single- component) and Type 2 (multi-component) behaviour. 5Pe 1 Samples from the upper part of the Main Andesites and the Upper Andesite (Fig. 2c, sites 6-7, 9 and 10) are characterized by almost single component and very stable magnetizations (Fig. 3a). The temperature unblocking spectra indicate magnetite (or low-titanium titanomagnetite, 500-580 "C) and haematite (>580 "C) as the chief remanence carriers. Directional stability is sometimes observed to 670"C, but more commonly samples display viscous behaviour above 640 "C. Both the Iapetus Ocean and Tornquist Sea therefore, which separated southern Britain from Laurentia and Baltica respectively in Ordovician times, were closed by Wenlock time. As Ordovician and Silurian palaeomagnetic data from Baltica and Eastern Avalonia now record a comparable northwards translation from high southerly to near-equatorial latitudes during this time, we postulate pre-Wenlock collision of these blocks to form BALONIA (Baltica + eastern Avalonia). After Conklin & Moore (1977). the Mesozoic units of northeast Mexico were variously deformed according to the position of their depositional areas with respect to the previously existing early upper Jurassic palaeogeographical elements (Fig. 1 a). Variations in the trend of the Sierra Madre Oriental fold belt can therefore be attributed to the shape of the Coahuila and Tamaulipas Peninsulas against which the Mesozoic strata of the Mexican Sea were buttressed by Laramide compressive forces acting from the southwest (Charleston 1981). For the most part. the Sierra Madre Oriental comprises deformed Mesozoic units, with a majority of the topographic high ground being formed by massive Cretaceous limestones (de Cserna 1956). The generalized stratigraphic column for the Cretaceous in the vicinity of Torreon (Fig. 2) shows the three units sampled in the present study. The Barremian- Aptian Cupido Limestone (Wilson 1977) was sampled at two locations, while the AIbian Aurora Limestone (Young 1977) and the medial Albian-early Cenomanian Cuesta del Cura Limestone (Ice & McNulty 1980) were sampled at one location each. Palaeomagnetic analyses of these samples identify a stable synfolding remanence at three localities that was acquired during the Laramide Orogeny (Eocene). The fourth locality exhibited a post-folding or late-synfolding remanence. This pole (Lat. = 69.9"N, Long. = 172.8"E, n = 27, k = 30, ag5 = 5.2") agrees well with a published Mexican Eocene pole position for a locality located 450 km north- northwest of the present study area. On the basis of this information, we conclude that a large fragment of northern Mexico has undergone a 10"-15" post-Eocene counterclockwise rotation

The fourth locality exhibited a post-folding or late-synfolding remanence. This pole (Lat. = 69.9"N, Long. = 172.8"E, n = 27, k = 30, ag5 = 5.2") agrees well with a published Mexican Eocene pole position for a locality located 450 km north- northwest of the present study area. Palaeomagnetic analyses of these samples identify a stable synfolding remanence at three localities that was acquired during the Laramide Orogeny (Eocene). The fourth locality exhibited a post-folding or late-synfolding remanence. Each locality has undergone a regional rotation and at least three localities have undergone local rotations since remanence acquisition. By examining the relation- ships between the apparent polar wander paths for North America and Mexico, pole positions generated by this study and observed structural trends, it has been possible to evaluate the different contributions of local versus regional rotations and to calculate a least-locally-rotated Eocene pole position for the Torreon region. This pole (Lat. = 69.9"N, Long. = 172.8"E, n = 27, k = 30, ag5 = 5.2") agrees well with a published Mexican Eocene pole position for a locality located 450 km north- northwest of the present study area. On the basis of this information, we conclude that a large fragment of northern Mexico has undergone a 10"-15" post-Eocene counterclockwise rotation

directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: ived 1992 April 27, in original form 1991 November 1 SUMMARY 122 oriented core samples were collected from folded Lower Cretaceous units at four localities in the Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains near Torreon, northeast Mexico. Palaeomagnetic analyses of these samples identify a stable synfolding remanence at three localities that was acquired during the Laramide Orogeny (Eocene). The fourth locality exhibited a post-folding or late-synfolding remanence. Each locality has undergone a regional rotation and at least three localities have undergone local rotations since remanence acquisition. The median destructive field (MDF) ranges between 10 mT and 40 mT. Because the thermal demagnetization method appeared to be more effective for removing magnetic overprint, the remaining specimens were treated by the thermal method. The characteristic direction of each specimen from the eight sites was determined by principal component analysis (Kirschvink 1980) using more than five points on the stepwise thermal demagnetization diagram. Only characteristic directions with MAD values less than 10" were used for the site-mean calculations (Table 2). This direction probably represents primary magnetization based on the lack of alteration of minerals (the thin section was examined for K-Ar dating), the stability of magnetization, and the high unblocking temperature of 600 "C. DISCUSSION The obtained K-Ar ages of the Chiopanshan volcanic rocks are in good agreement with those based on palaeontological studies. The volcanic rocks of the Chiopanshan stage are intercalated with the strata of the Nanchuang Formation (Ho 1988). This formation belongs to the N14 to N16 planktonic foraminifera1 zones defined by Blow (1969) and to the NN8 to NNlO calcareous nannofossil zones by Martini (1971): (Huang & Huang 1984). These zones are assigned to the interval between 13 Ma and 8 Ma. Thus, our K-Ar ages of

e volcanic rocks represents a reliable and realistic palaeomagnetic direction of Miocene age. The geomagnetic secular variation is averaged out in the mean calculation for the palaeomagnetic direction, because our directions are obtained from rocks with ages from early to late Miocene, covering at least two polarity epochs of normal and reversed. In northern Taiwan, Hsu el a/. (1966) observed northerly palaeomagnetic directions in the basaltic lavas of the Chiopanshan stage, and Lee et af. (1991) reported southerly directions with small clockwise deflection from the Miocene sedimentary rocks. The former data were obtained without thermal demagnetization and principal component analysis. In the latter study, detailed information concerning to the thermal of AF demagnetization experiments on the magnetic stability was not provided. These data passed neither the reversal test nor the fold test. We therefore suggest that these data are less reliable than our data and accordingly we did not combine the palaeomagnetic data of Hsu et af. (1966) and Lee et af. (1991) with our new data. We compared the palaeomagnetic pole position obtained from northern Taiwan in this study with the Neogene pole position for the Asian continent (Fig. 4). Reconstruction of the 10Ma palaeoposition of Taiwan and the south Ryukyu arc implies that the cusp shape at the arc junction has already existed prior to 10 Ma. As we show below the analysis of results of thermal demagnetization has indeed confirmed such a remanence structure. The most common magnetization found in rocks of the British and Irish Caledonides is the so-called B magnetization, according to terminology adopted for the assumed oldest component in Scottish Old Red Sandstone rocks (e.g. Storetvedt & Carmichael 1979; Storetvedt et a/. 1990). The B remanence has shallow inclination (~10"); it is characterized by a dual-polarity structure but the reverse component normally predominates. However, a second magnetization, termed the A component, with southerly declination and shallow upward (approximately -20") inclination, has been iden- tified in a number of British mid-Palaeozoic rocks. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS The Ordos basin is the largest Mesozoic non-marine interior sedimentary basin in the NCB. Some 85 per cent of the basin has been covered by Quaternary loess. Geological investigations of this basin demonstrate that it has been stable with respect to western Pacific tectonic belts since the Permian (Ren et al. 1990). Lower Cretaceous continental sediments of the Zhidan Group are well developed in the southwestern part of the Ordos basin where they have a total thickness of up to 2000 m (Ha0 et al. 1986). According to extensive palaeontological research, the sediment series in the Binxian area consists of six formations. This series is composed mainly of red and purple to grey sandstone, mudstone interbedded with conglomerates, and purple mudstone and argillaceous sandstone in the lower part. The middle part includes interbedded grey mudstone, ar- gillaceous sandstone and sandstone, grading upward to grey-yellow massive arkosic sandstone interbedded with siltstone. These sediments contain abundant ostracods, plant fossils and vertebrates such as Lycoptera sp., Sinamia zdanskyi Stensio, Sinemys sp., Eotomistoma multidentato Young, Psittacosaurus sp. and Protoceratopus sp., which are indicative of an Early Cretaceous age (Shaanxi Regional Stratig

Received 1993 April 19; in original form 1992 November 4 SUMMARY Sediments of Devonian age located in three areas of North Africa have been affected to different degrees by the Hercynian Orogeny. They show various remagnetizations of Carboniferous, Permian and Pleistocene age. In the Ben-Zireg anticline near the Variscan front in Algeria, the main phase of magnetic overprint- ing occurs during the Tournaisian. It is superimposed on a Famennian primary direction carried by magnetite. In the Bhi-Abbks area to the South of the Variscan belt, griotte limestones of Famennian age show a strong recent remagnetization with few residual Permian directions. As the position of the CB pole is over 30" away from the CV pole revealed from the Comerong Volcanics of similar age in the Tasman Fold Belt, southeastern Australia, Hurley & Van der Voo (1987) suggested that the CV pole is more likely to be erroneous because of the tectonic uncertainty of its source region. However, this view has been refuted by other workers based on either geological or palaeomagnetic arguments (e.g. Schmidt et al. 1986; Schmidt, Embleton & Palmer 1987; Kent & May 1987; Li, Schmidt & Embleton 1988; Li et al. 1990). They suggested instead that the age of the CB pole could be y

ither geological or palaeomagnetic arguments (e.g. Schmidt et al. 1986; Schmidt, Embleton & Palmer 1987; Kent & May 1987; Li, Schmidt & Embleton 1988; Li et al. 1990). They suggested instead that the age of the CB pole could be younger than the age of the rocks from which it was determined. Subsidence of the Windermere Group basement exceeded the supply of available sediment by Early Silurian time, resulting in graptolite-bearing mudstones and siltstones throughout Llandovery and Wenlock time (Early Silurian). The majority of these sediments are gray, with their contained iron reduced during burial. Some are black finely laminated mudstones, taken to indicate deposition as well as diagenesis in anoxic waters. By contrast, the red beds contain oxidized iron in the form of haematite. They occur in localized lenticular units up to 20rn thick and several kilometres across. Contained graptolites and trilobites confirm their deep marine origin (Rickards 1978; Hemsley 1978). This anomalous facies is sporadically present in other Llandovery sequences in the CaledonianJAppalachian orogen, and has been attributed to increased supply of detrital haematite during eustatic marine transgressions (Ziegler & McKerrow 1975). Clastic supply to the Windermere Group increased progressively during Late Silurian time, probably in a foreland basin developed to the south of the overriding Laurentian continent (Kneller 1991). The basin was filled to sea-level by latest Silurian time and probably had an Early Devonian non-marine history. However, this uppermost part of the sequence was uplifted and totally eroded during the Acadian Orogeny, which culminated in late Early to Mid-Devonian time (review by Soper, Webb & Woodcock 1987). Received 1993 May 21; in original form 1992 November 3 SUMMARY High unblocking temperature magnetization components carried by haematite have been isolated from 12 sites of Llandovery (Lower Silurian) red mudstones from NW England. The principal deformation phase in this area is Acadian (mid-Devonian), however, some faults (with related folds) were also active during the later Variscan orogeny. The site-mean magnetization directions pass a regional fold test at the 95 per cent confidence level, implying that the magnetization components pre-date Acadian folding. The overall mean direction (Declination: 43.4", Inclination: -24.1", 12.4") gives a pole position at 13.6"S, 313.9"E and a palaeolatitude of 12"s. The low palaeolatitude implies closure of the Iapetus Ocean between Eastern Avalonia and Laurentia by Late Llandovery time and is consistent with a recently published palaeolatitude (13"s) for the Wenlock (mid-Silurian) of southern Britain. Comparison of these values with the published palaeolatitude from NW England of 43"s for Caradoc (Late Ordovician) time implies very rapid (at leas

adoc (Late Ordovician) time implies very rapid (at least 15 cm yr-') northward drift of Eastern Avalonia during Late Ordovician/Early Silurian time. The new pole position from the Llandovery red beds lies close to Late Silurian and Early Devonian poles from Scotland and Wales, but is significantly different from a group of mid-Silurian poles comprising data from Scottish intrusions and from Swedish sediments. This discrepancy may be due to Late SilurianfEarly Devonian (pre-Acadian) remagnetization of our sampling sites, or local clockwise rotation of the sampling sites during Acadian and/or Variscan deformation. However, the positive fold test, presence of reversals and local deformation history tend to mitigate against these possibilities. The more likely interpretation is that although Baltica/Scotland were one continental block from the mid-Silurian (Scandian orogeny), Eastern Avalonia did not become part of this block until latest Silurian. Before any demagnetization analysis, samples were put in a zero field for one month in order to reduce spurious viscous components. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the specimens so cleaned was analysed using a spinner magnetometer JR4 (GEOFYZIKA, Brno). First, several pilot specimens were subjected to stepwise alternating field and thermal demagnetization in order to get information about their magnetic behaviour. The alternating field treatment did not allow a complete demagnetization, hence, the thermal procedure was applied to all specimens. After each heating step, low-field magnetic susceptibility was measured at room temperature on a KL Y2 Kappabridge (GEOFYZIKA, Brno) in order to detect any mineralogical phase changes. This last procedure was performed in steps varying from 150 oc at low temperatures to 10 °C at the highest to obtain a more detailed evolution of the remanence. Eleven sites yielded reliable magnetic directions, with analysis of the results using standard principal component and great circle analyses. Up to three directions of magnetiza­ tion can be identified in these rocks. The first, termed A, is generally removed below 200 °C, although in some cases it persists up to 450 oc in the volcanic rocks. It is approximately parallel to the present-day Earth's magnetic field in the study area (Dec/Inc 360° /67°) and is thus thought to be of recent origin. The second direction identified, termed B, is isolated at intermediate blocking temperatures (150-350 °C), and yields an overall in situ mean direction of 195°/8°, k=22.3, a 95 =13.1° (seven sites). These directions fail the fold test of McFadden (1990), and correspond to a palaeopole position of 34°S; 356°E. This coincides with the Late Carboniferous sector of the European apparent polar wander path, and thus the B direction is interpreted as being a secondary overprint of this age. The highest blocking temperature direction, termed C, is identified at temperatures between 350° and 450-600 °C. Received 1993 March 15; in original form 1992 September 18 INTRODUCTION SUMMARY Apparently conflicting data within the palaeomagnetic database suggest that Bohemia was at much shallower palaeolatitudes than the Armorican and Iberian massifs in Ordovician times. In order to resolve this controversy a palaeomagnetic study of Arenig and Llanvirn volcanic and sedimentary rocks from the Barrandfan Basin, Central Bohemia has been carried out. This basin comprises a sequence of unmetamorphosed Lower Palaeozoic rocks, the main folding of which occurred in Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous times. The samples collected (l} sites, 153 samples) were subjected to stepwise thermal and alternating field treatment. Eleven sites yielded reliable magnetic directions, with analysis of the results using standard principal component and great circle analyses. Up to three directions of magnetiza­ tion can be identified in these rocks. The first, termed A, is generally removed below 200 °C, although in some cases it persists up to 450 oc in the volcanic rocks. It is approximately parallel to the present-day Earth's magnetic field in the study area (Dec/Inc 360° /67°) and is thus thought to be of recent origin. The second direction identified, termed B

vetian, rocks which comprise pre­ dominantly shales and carbonates, with the first carbonate rocks appearing in Mid-Silurian times (Havlicek 1981). The most important phase of volcanic activity during the Ordovician of the Barrandian Basin was initiated in the Tremadoc under shallow marine conditions, and lasted almost uninterrupted until Early to Mid-Arenig times. This resulted in the basic explosive-effusive Komarov complex which is up to 1000 m in thickness. This complex was formed by fissure eruptions along a trend which ran at an angle to the main axis of the basin, reviving pre-Ordovician Cadomian structures (Havlicek 1981). Samples from Upper Arenig and Lower Llanvirn sediments and interbedded volcanic rocks in the Barrandian Basin were collected, the localities of which are shown in Fig. 1, and the lithologies are listed in Table 1. Since the pioneering work of Barrande in the 19th century, these fossiliferous sediments have been extensively studied and the biostratigraphic ages are well established. Received 1993 March 15; in original form 1992 September 18 INTRODUCTION SUMMARY Apparently conflicting data within the palaeomagnetic database suggest that Bohemia was at much shallower palaeolatitudes than the Armorican and Iberian massifs in Ordovician times. In order to resolve this controversy a palaeomagnetic study of Arenig and Llanvirn volcanic and sedimentary rocks from the Barrandfan Basin, Central Bohemia has been carried out. This basin comprises a sequence of unmetamorphosed Lower Palaeozoic rocks, the main folding of which occurred in Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous times. The samples collected (l} sites, 153 samples) were subjected to stepwise thermal and alternating field treatment. Eleven sites yielded reliable magnetic directions, with analysis of the results using standard principal component and great circle analyses. Up to three directions of magnetiza­ tion can be identified in these rocks. The first, termed A, is generally removed below 200 °C, although in some cases it persists up to 450 oc in the volcanic rocks. It is approximately parallel to the present-day Earth's magnetic field in the study area (Dec/Inc 360° /67°) and is thus thought to be of recent origin. The second direction identified, termed B

vetian, rocks which comprise pre­ dominantly shales and carbonates, with the first carbonate rocks appearing in Mid-Silurian times (Havlicek 1981). The most important phase of volcanic activity during the Ordovician of the Barrandian Basin was initiated in the Tremadoc under shallow marine conditions, and lasted almost uninterrupted until Early to Mid-Arenig times. This resulted in the basic explosive-effusive Komarov complex which is up to 1000 m in thickness. This complex was formed by fissure eruptions along a trend which ran at an angle to the main axis of the basin, reviving pre-Ordovician Cadomian structures (Havlicek 1981). Samples from Upper Arenig and Lower Llanvirn sediments and interbedded volcanic rocks in the Barrandian Basin were collected, the localities of which are shown in Fig. 1, and the lithologies are listed in Table 1. Since the pioneering work of Barrande in the 19th century, these fossiliferous sediments have been extensively studied and the biostratigraphic ages are well established. The structure of these Lower Palaeozoic rocks is fairly simple, with the Lower Cambrian to Givetian rocks forming a gently dipping syncline, unconformably overlain by Westphalian age sediments. At 10 sites, a high blocking temperature characteristic remanence carried by haematite was isolated. This remanence is shown to predate probable early Devonian folding. Anti-parallel north- and south-directed remanences through a 100 m section of redbeds and a positive conglomerate test on haematite-bearing volcanic clasts suggest absence of remagnetization. Inverting the south-directed sites and unfolding yields a characteristic remanence with a mean declination of 23.6" and a mean inclination of - 14.2" (myg5 = 7.3", k = 45.4). e find no significant difference between early Silurian palaeolatitudes for central Newfoundland north and south of the Red Indian Line suture, and conclude that the part of the Iapetus Ocean across the suture had narrowed to less than about 5" by the early Silurian. This is consistent with palaeomagnetic results from Britain and Ireland that suggest no more than a narrow Iapetus at low palaeolatitude by the early Silurian. We also tested whether we have underestimated palaeolatitude because of sediment compaction reducing remanence inclination from that of the early Silurian field. We measured anisotropy of the isothermal remanence (IRM) acquisition for one specimen from each stable site, finding that a field of 200 to 800 rnT applied at 45" to bedding produced an isothermal remanence oriented on average at 42" to bedding. Theory then predicts that sediment compaction caused less than 2" average inclination shallowing in the Springdale Group redbeds, and less than a 1" underestimation of palaeolatitude. The Cainozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Australia reflects a progressive northward drift of the continent from moderately high southern latitudes in the Cretaceous period. It provides a method for age-dating and a reference for studying the movement of terranes on the margins of the Australian plate. Most parts of the APWP are spatially well defined by poles from sediments, basalts and poorly age-controlled laterites (Idnurm 1985). The time-scale for the APWP is, however, fixed by only five dated poles, placing a high reliance on the precision and accuracy of each pole. Least constrained is the Palaeogene part of the APWP which contains only two poles, one at 26Ma near the beginning of the period and the other at 58Ma near the end (Idnurm 1985)-a time gap of about 30 Myr. The present study aimed to fill the Palaeogene gap with a Late Eocene pole from the Browns Creek Formation of the Otway Basin. This sedimentary formation satisfies two conditions essential for precise time-calibration: a well- defined age and a remanence acquired over a sufficiently long period to record a time-averaged field. The second requirement is not satisfied by rocks such as single lava flows or groups of flows extruded during short episodes of volcanism, which record the

The second requirement is not satisfied by rocks such as single lava flows or groups of flows extruded during short episodes of volcanism, which record the direction of the geomagnetic field over brief time intervals (e.g. McElhinny 1973). These volcanics give an estimate of the position of the geomagnetic pole, which is subject to secular variations and is, therefore, unsuitable as a stable geographic reference. Palaeomagnetism assumes that, over a sufficiently long period, the time-averaged geomagnetic pole (i.e. the palaeomagnetic pole) coincides approximately with the geographic pole. (The agreement is generally unlikely to be better than a few degrees because the time-averaged geomagnetic field is not perfectly dipolar; e.g. Merrill & McElhinny 1983.) For Australia, the amplitude of secular variations is comparable to the net Tertiary apparent polar wander. For example, the present geomagnetic field (declination 5", inclination -56O) at Alice Springs near the centre of the continent, would yield a geomagnetic pole that is displaced from the geographic pole by 14O-nearly half the angular span of the Cainozoic APWP. section_candidates.excerpt: om Palaeocene to Oligo-Miocene. However, new palaeomagnetic data from additional sites on Tertiary magmatic rocks of the western Greek Rhodope show declination values indicating, in most cases, a clockwise rotation, whereas inclinations are systematically lower than those corresponding to the actual latitudinal position of the Rhodope. Our results, together with previously published ones, are discussed in the light of recent ideas proposed for the Rhodope and the north Aegean region. We suggest that at least the western part of the Greek Rhodope has been clockwise rotated after the Oligocene. North-south to NE-SW extension tilted the formations towards the north or north-east, producing apparently high inclinations, if the alternative pole position for Eurasia proposed by Westphal (1990) is adopted. INTRODUCTION There are still controversies concerning the origin, the age and the geodynamic role of the Rhodope massif of northern Greece. The succession in this area is summarized in Table 1 and unconformably overlies (Lower Cambrian to Middle Ordovician) rocks belonging to the Choseon Supergroup. It commences with red or drab detrital sediments of the Manhang Formation ranging from siltstones to fine-pebble conglomerates; samples from the red facies comprise an important component of this study (Table 1). The variety of lithologies in the succeeding Kuncheon Formation include coal measures but are considered generally unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Coal-bearing cyclothems also occur in the overlying rocks of the Changseong Formation which contains a Permian plant flora and is succeeded by the mainly arenitic sandstones of the Hambaeksan Formation. Although a Recent field overprint widely recorded in Korean rocks is represented here, an ancient field component structure is recovered from the red bed facies in this Supergroup by detailed thermal demagnetization. The succession in this area is summarized in Table 1 and unconformably overlies (Lower Cambrian to Middle Ordovician) rocks belonging to the Choseon Supergroup. It commences with red or drab detrital sediments of the Manhang Formation ranging from siltstones to fine-pebble conglomerates; samples from the red facies comprise an important component of this study (Table 1). The variety of lithologies in the succeeding Kuncheon Formation include coal measures but are considered generally unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study.
